abstract: Democratic backsliding is often framed as a contest between defenders and disruptors of democratic institutions. That framing can miss a third response, withholding punishment from disruptors while penalizing defenders who confront them. We model the three responses as strategies in an evolutionary game, track their shares with replicator dynamics, and assume defenders beat disruptors head-to-head but have a payoff disadvantage among non-punishers even when disruptors are absent. If the third response cannot spread among disruptors, a payoff condition draws the population toward the classical May--Leonard heteroclinic cycle, a rock--paper--scissors succession in which disruption repeatedly becomes rare, then widespread. If that response can, a threshold on its payoff advantage over disruptors determines whether all three coexist or defenders alone vanish. In finite-population simulations, sustained resurgence requires reintroducing lost strategies. Our contribution is to show how two separately documented political tendencies, if combined, can sustain disruption despite defenders' head-to-head advantage over disruptors.
